content.intro: Learn relationships between models through a compact visual, an inspectable Django example, and a practical verification task.
content.why_it_matters: Relationships Between Models matters because a Django project has to behave predictably across requests, database state, configuration, and deployments. Understanding this piece makes the surrounding application easier to test, maintain, and secure.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: This lesson examines relationships between models as part of django models and database fundamentals. The objective is to understand the behavior, connect it to the listed subtopics, and verify it with a small example rather than relying on memorized syntax.

content_blocks.title: What to cover
content_blocks.text: The source syllabus for this lesson names: ForeignKey; OneToOneField; ManyToManyField; Forward and reverse relations; Choosing suitable relationship models. Keep these distinct concepts together: know what each item does, when it applies, and what assumption must be verified in your project.

items.title: ForeignKey
items.text: `ForeignKey` models a many-to-one relationship, such as many books referencing one author. Choose the related name and deletion policy to reflect the domain.

items.title: OneToOneField
items.text: OneToOneField affects persistence and data correctness. Keep invariants in validation and database constraints where appropriate, inspect generated SQL/migrations, and test both expected data and error/rollback behavior.

items.title: ManyToManyField
items.text: ManyToManyField affects persistence and data correctness. Keep invariants in validation and database constraints where appropriate, inspect generated SQL/migrations, and test both expected data and error/rollback behavior.

items.title: Forward and reverse relations
items.text: For Forward and reverse relations, identify the Django component responsible, the inputs and outputs it owns, and the boundary conditions that matter. Use the accompanying example as a starting point, verify it with the official versioned documentation, and record one test demonstrating expected behavior.

items.title: Choosing suitable relationship models
items.text: Choosing suitable relationship models affects persistence and data correctness. Keep invariants in validation and database constraints where appropriate, inspect generated SQL/migrations, and test both expected data and error/rollback behavior.

content_blocks.title: Worked example: Relationships Between Models
content_blocks.expected_output: Each book references one author; author.books exposes the reverse relation. PROTECT prevents deleting an author while books refer to them.

content_blocks.title: Guided walkthrough
content_blocks.text: First identify the input and the responsible Django component. Next trace how the example moves through “Relationships Between Models” and the related concept “ForeignKey”. Predict the result before running or inspecting it. Finally compare the observed behavior with the expected result and the cited official documentation.

content_blocks.title: Try it yourself
content_blocks.text: Change one input or configuration choice related to ForeignKey. Write down the expected outcome, test one normal case and one invalid or boundary case, then record what changed. Do not add real credentials or sensitive production data.

content_blocks.title: Common mistakes and fixes
content_blocks.text: Common pitfalls include skipping a required configuration/import, copying a fragment without its model or URL context, trusting client input, or treating a development-only behavior as production-ready. Check the earliest failing assumption, consult the version-specific docs, and add a regression test for the failure you found.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: You should now be able to describe relationships between models, explain the listed topics, inspect the example, and choose an appropriate verification step. Keep the scope and version caveat visible when sharing your solution.
